review:
The music alone is worth it. A perfect example of how game play can elevate an already incredible element, and vice-versa. 

Only downside is my neck kind of hurts from all the HEADBANGING GIVE ME THE SOUNDTRACK NOW YOU COWARDS I NEED IT
The developers are the CIA, the game is crack, and I'm a minority in America during the 80s.

I have one SERIOUS complaint about this game that my review will cover. Beyond that complaint, this game is AMAZING.
If you like heavy metal. Buy this game.
If you enjoy boomer shooters. Buy this game.
If you enjoy rhythm games. Buy this game.
The team has remained dedicated to it and just decided to drop a free DLC/Update that continues the main story in a new mode. It's an amazing team with an amazing passion and dedication to this beautiful game. And I am so happy I bought it. The soundtrack alone is worth the price.

So my main complaint. That holds this game back from being one of the greatest games I have ever played.

The way they do the Score Multiplier.

Attack on the beat, kill on beat, and do slaughters (glory kills from DOOM) and the multiplier goes up. On a scale of x1, x2, x4, x8, and caps at x16. Miss a beat or get hit by an enemy and it goes down. It also goes down over time on its own. Encouraging you to constantly be moving and fighting. Since it tracks your score and has a leader board the multiplier makes sense. Play well, get more points, and get a high score. Simple. Rewards good play.

HOWEVER, EVERYTHING is tied to the multiplier. How fast your character moves (which feels a little slow for a DOOM/Boomer Shooter like game). How much damage you do. Even the music. Is tied to the multiplier. And the soundtrack is amazing with some great vocalists that put their heart into the songs. And the lyrics of each song help tell the story of the game. BUT you can only hear those lyrics if you keep a 16x multiplier. Which is a shame because the soundtrack is such a shinning point of the game. And you hear less and less of it the lower your multiplier. And since the enemies have some SERIOUS tracking. you can dodge behind a ranged enemy and it will snap its spine to spin and still hit you. And you'll be beamed from across the arena. Or have fly enemies lob three slowing projectiles on different beats and track you with each shot. Get hit once and your multiplier drops. If you were at a x16 you get downed to a x8, lose the lyrics that you were rocking to. Now dealing less damage. And get completely thrown off your grove and not in an enjoyable way.

The game is hard (especially on higher difficulties). And I enjoy that about it. I enjoy the combat. The flow it can have. A beautiful story to tell. And rocking out to the soundtrack all the while.

I just HATE that everything is tied to that multiplier. Keep the multiplier in. Reward good play with a higher score. Make it go down if I get hit. I agree with that. Just don't strip me of this great music and serious firepower because I slipped up once. Or dodged one enemy just to get domed by a cambian hiding in the corner. I'd be so much more invested to sticking through the hard parts of the game if I could just keep the music going endlessly and rock out. (No, I am not going to play it via youtube or whatever. Because the music is synced to each level, looping or progressing as needed while you move through each level. It's very well done).

Buy this game. Enjoy it. And if you are looking for that high score be prepared for some tough times. End rant, thanks for reading.

For Steam deck owners; This runs great (through the first few levels at least) and is a blast to play.

Edit: I have played through a much more significant amount of the game entirely on steam deck and have never dropped below 35 fps  (usually a stable 40 with only a couple sections being more demanding) and have thoroughly enjoyed both the music and the game the entire time.

I keep seeing people calling this game a BPM clone but It really isn't. I found on BPM's community page that a developer for the game confirmed the Metal: Hellsinger team did not copy them and they were actually working on their game for the same amount of time. He also stated that they're all friends and I think the BPM guys actually shared some of their ideas with them during development. https://imgur.com/a/vAf8WCd

Anyways I've been extremely excited for this game to release ever since I played BPM, which i'm sure most players can relate. Combining my two most favorite game genres into one didn't really seem possible until I discovered it and of course I genuinely loved it, so seeing Metal: Hellsinger on the horizon got me hyped. But I seem to have a tendency to overhype games a little lol.

My only problem is that I was really hoping this game would have roguelike aspects similar to BPM but instead you play on 8 set in stone levels (not including torments). This isn't exactly terrible but It kinda destroys any replay-ability unless you like grinding leaderboard scores. Also the game is pretty short. I was able to 100% the game in about 5 hours and tbh I feel like this is just because of how easy it is. If dying 20 times is one of the 5 rarest achievements in the game (5% of players) then you can assume its not exactly hard. I don't really like some design choices either. You fight the same boss at the end of every level with the same boss music, and most enemies aren't exactly creative either. Every map starts to blend together in my head because there's nothing really unique about any of them. The story isn't great either but I really didn't even expect one. I never really experienced any bugs except sometimes AI pathfinding would break and the enemies would just get stuck in place on terrain. None of this really destroys the game or takes away from the experience though, they're really just minor gripes that I have.

Overall this game is a massive step up from BPM in most places. Lots of problems in BPM were solved here but there are also lots of good things from BPM that are missing. At the end of the day they are two separate games that are both worth playing.

One of those games where the "$1 for one hour of fun" rule doesn't QUITE hold up. Because the game is SUPER fun, as in, I'm having more fun with this than I did on a run of Doom. 

But it is pretty short. I left the game on AFK for a while, and so I'd only actually played about an hour and a half, and I've done half the levels + challenges. And it's true, the bosses are a little repetitive. Maybe the point isn't to confuse the player too much, since timing gunplay and dodging to a rhythm in a fast paced shooter is pretty difficult. That said, the game's (limited) length keeps it from really wearing out before you can finish the game, which is good in a roundabout kind of way. It's also probably more enjoyable if you don't just blast it all in one sitting.

I would LOVE to see more content added to this game, because the system is amazing, so long as the new content innovates on the system with different interactions of rhythm. It's a winning foundation, now build on it.

Also the story/narrator doesn't really hit with me and feels very tacked on, but whatever, nobody played Doom for the story either.

I'm going to be honest. Don't have the negative review dissuade you from buying it, but read on if you want my reasoning for why I would strictly not recommend it outright.

TL;DR: Metal: Hellsinger has everything it needs to be a fantastic release on the art and music side, but falls short in the rhythm and gameplay aspects.

I have about 60 hours in the game's [strike] sibling [/strike] only other counterpart, BPM: Bullets Per Minute, and have been an avid FPS gamer for longer than a decade now. This game's music is fantastic, the scoring system is great, the little side challenges hearken back to the Doom 2016 relic challenges and the Doom Eternal Slayer Gates. The weapons and viewmodel animations are fantastic.

The gameplay, however is lacking a lot. Movement feels floaty, and after certain actions you lose all of your momentum seemingly from nothing. 

Firing and reloading your weapons isn't satisfying at all in comparison to similar games (BPM, Doom Eternal, etc,). It lacks the "little" touches. The noises that the reloads make, the non-overt animations, the fact that the guns barely stand out from the environment do the design a disservice. The shotgun racking automatically, reloading automatically finishing whether or not you hit the active reload timing, and other little "game does it for you" mechanics, while accessible, takes a lot out of the feeling of the "shoot on the beat" style gameplay, These are small things that add up to... really not a very satisfying game feel and a slightly boring gameplay loop overall. My biggest, 1000% largest gripe with the arsenal so far (Having unlocked all weapons) is that the Vulcan does rocket jumps, yes it does. Rocket Jumping feels flaccid. Rocket jumping feeling flaccid is probably the worst thing I can think of to put in a game, it's so feast or famine. Either its really good because its fun and effective, or you're better off not implementing the mechanic. Here, its the latter.

[b] Past this point, minor spoilers [/b]

The enemy types are also a pain to deal with. You have the generic fodder enemies that serve as health refills if you glory kill them, the generic ranged enemy that has a weak melee attack when you get close. The generic tank enemy that's slow, deals a lot of damage and has a gap closer. And the generic shield enemy that (for some ungodly reason) does more damage and has a higher HP total than the normal ranged enemy with a shield that you have to bypass to deal damage.

Other enemy types are lifted straight from Doom 2016 and Doom Eternal in terms of enemy design. The Stalkers are Prowlers. The Heirophants are Summoners. The different between Metal: Hellsinger's encounter design and Doom 2016 and Eternal encounter design is that Doom's encounters were peppered with fodder to replenish resources and all of the other enemies were specialized enough to make target priority a real thing. A pinky would always rank higher than an imp, unless the imp was charging a big fireball. Here... it's kind of take care of what's in front of you? Behemoths are easily kited, which is fine but there's no real threat from a fast enemy. I'm not saying the Stalker is fast, I'm saying the Stalker just teleports where it wants to. There's nothing that really rushes the player down, trying to either corner them or force them to take a hit from the behemoth. Shield Cambions are a pain. You know how dangerous Shield guys in Doom are? You know how you can overload their shields with energy weapons? Yeah no, here its just get behind them. You know Guardians from BPM? You know how you can either get behind them if you're quick or you can wait for their downtime after their attack? Yeah no, here its just get behind them or just spam sword attacks until they die.

A slight boost in the player's walking speed would also make the enemies less annoying to deal with. I can't tell you how many times I got clipped in arenas by an Eyeless because the aoe is way too large and the player moves way too goddamn slow.

The bossfights so far, the first 4 hells, which are the ones I've played, are very lackluster as well. It can actually be boiled down into four steps: Introduction > Add Wave > Bullet Hell > Repeat at step 2. There's almost no rhythm to the bosses, or any of the enemies for that matter, and they kind of just do whatever whenever. This would be absolutely fine, had BPM not been released two years ago. If you've ever played, think Draugr. Draugr is a fantastic implementation of the rhythm mechanic in a boss fight. Slow projectiles, fast projectiles, floor AOE, side cleaves where you have to dodge left or right, and an adds attack that is dangerous enough to get you to clear them ASAP but not annoying enough to break the flow of the whole fight. 

Here, the boss says "I'm going to vomit projectiles, then I'm going to go invulnerable to give you a wave of adds, then I'll go back to vomiting projectiles." [b] That is a very weak boss fight in my honest opinion. [/b] Give me mechanics that actually matter. Make me juggle those mechanics with an add wave of smaller units. A boss arena is a stage for the boss, not for the boss to go take a water break 2 minutes into the performance for a can-can dance.

That's it, if I go any farther I'll ramble on and on about how disappointing this game has been so far.

The only problem is that since it's a rhythm game, the song structures don't allow for a very elaborate soundtrack. The songs are a little samey, so things can get repetitive pretty quickly if you don't take it easy.

And since it's a rhythm game, don't expect this to be a alternative for Doom Eternal and the like. It's not. The appeal may overlap in some ways, but the level of mechanical demand is quite different and although it may seem similar on the surface, the experience is not the same.

But either way, it's a pretty awesome game. If it clicks with you, it's worth every penny.

In an industry that often prioritizes bloated games with no cohesive design, Metal: Hellsinger bursts in with a screeching guitar riff and shows everyone how it’s done! It pitches an appealing premise--that of a rhythm FPS--and proceeds to deliver on it while effortlessly avoiding the rot that weighs down many games today. 

The result is five ridiculously entertaining hours of headbanging action, supercharged by an adrenaline-pumping soundtrack featuring a star-studded lineup of old and new Metalheads alike. And you know what? The story ain’t too bad, either, and is told with an enjoyable amount of style and personality.

Metal: Hellsinger, as a whole, is polished, innovative, unpretentious, and most importantly fun, and the industry could certainly use more games like it. I [i]absolutely[/i] love it, and I strongly recommend you check it out.

Playing this game feels better than jerking off. 

Its a banger from beginning to the end.

They nailed the music and aesthetics, with an absolutely loaded cast of vocalists and tracks, and got the core mechanics of the game right, but failed to really pull together the ideas here into a cohesive game. It just feels disjointed

Take for example the central mechanic of the beat. While you operate on the rules of following the beat, the enemies are basically standard doom-like enemies you could see in any game that the devs elected to not have follow any such rules at all. While I understand something like this would've taken a ton of time and resources, it really can feel off to have everything in the game going at the pace of the music except the enemies.

The hit streak counter also feels like the game is actively discouraging you from using certain tools. Both the sword and the shotgun are fun to use and effective weapons. I especially love the swords ultimate. But they have tied the hit streak counter to not only not missing beats, but not getting hit, and enemy tells in this game are not exactly the best, especially up close. This effectively reinforces run and gun gameplay and encourages long range weapon use instead of diving in with close range weapons, as the hit streak, more than just giving score, gives buffs and bonuses, which you essentially can easily throw away by going in close range and relying on slaughters to restore health and keep you going. I think the reward for going hitless and the reward for consistently keeping on beat should've been separate. They don't work well together.

Torments are another problem. At their core, the challenges can feel legitimately interesting and challenging. But more often than not, you find yourself wasting time looking for enemies who spawn on the edges of these maps, and stay there, oftentimes stuck on the terrain or simply standing there. And the restart loop for failure is a bit longer than I would have liked. Instant retries on challenges like this are a must, but instead, we have to listen to the narrator speak for around 5 seconds, watch a score meter go up (In a mode where anything but the completed challenge is essentially meaningless), and then hit restart. It's easier just to pause right before you fail and hit restart.

Speaking of the narrator, he VERY quickly outstays his welcome. The voicework itself is great. But I can hardly think of any game that has benefited from near constant narration and one liners from a single character, and this is no exception. You will find yourself tiring of the narration quite quickly.

Another thing you will find yourself tired of very quickly is the boss encounters. While each has a little mechanic or two here or there in an attempt to keep fresh, it tends to fall flat. Each boss follows virtually the same pattern of firing off projectiles before engaging in their unique mechanic before summoning a wave of enemies. Just like the designs of the fights themselves, all of them are near identical visually with just slight differences.

That isn't to say there isn't anything good about this game. The core loop of trying to shoot, dodge, and reload on the beat is pretty inherently fun. While it can vary by each individuals taste, I personally love the vocal lineup, being stacked with some of my favorite metal vocalists of all time. The inclusion of soilwork singer Bjorn Strid was especially a nice surprise. 

But it feels as though the developers did not properly synchronize design choices across mechanics, and the repetition will kick in before the end of the second hour. At 30$, it can be a good buy if you really are itching for something different in a rhythm game or a shooter, or are a fan of metal as a genre as I am, but if any of those things are untrue of you, I would recommend skipping.

My favorite implementation of the rhythm game genre is when you're not tied to any prescribed button sequences, but you can jam out to the music in whatever way you please. Hellsinger delivers this, while being a pretty fun PvE shooter on top of it. The bullet hell aspect takes some getting used to in first person, but there are never so many ranged enemies that it gets overwhelming.
And then of course there's the music. Obviously if you hate metal, this isn't the game for you, but if you like it, oh boy are there some killer songs in here. That first time you get your combo to 16x and the lyrics set in... downright electrifying!

[h1] DOOM: BPM [/h1]

Metal: Hellsinger was a pleasant surprise. I'm already so burnt-out by 'Early Access Retro indie FPS, Quake-inspired games, set in a (insert typical aesthetic here), with 1 weapon gimmick, dumb AI, boring maps... that'll be $19.99 please' type games.
Sorry, I just have like ~40 boomer-shooters in my library, and I can't distinguish them anymore.
So with Metal: Hellsinger, it was a truly neat surprise. It was a nice change of form, and finally something which felt like striked out & carved something really unique & cool.



[h1] A Pure Metal Rhythm Shooter [/h1]

Straight-up, I suck at rhythms in video-games. I'm typically piss at most rhythm games, and timing each note right. Which made it a hefty indecisive choice as to whether I even wanted to play this game. Yet it looked really nice, and there seemed to be some very interesting mechanics & systems outside of the rhythm game-play as well.
The neat mechanic to skip reloads through a well-timed beat was really cool, and is something that couldn't really work in any other game. Albeit I think that it'd've been truly cool if you could skip reloads through dashing too, and not just pressing the reload button. When I first noticed that dashing could be in-beat with the rhythm, I actually thought it was done for exactly that. It could cause some insanely smart strategies for high-skill players I can imagine.

Each demon is cool, and they're all unique. There are no demon where they feel like fillers, or bloats, or anything. They all seem to fit into the game-play loop of the game, and feel very fine-tuned to the pacing of it all. They're also not brainless either, even if they're not super smart too. They have a nice middle-ground somewhere between ULTRAKILL & DOOM Eternal's demons; but it earns that through lessening the demon aggressiveness & smartness by scaling up the difficulty of attention too. The mere rhythm aspect of the game make it indirectly a lot harder than controlling something like the Doom Slayer, for example. One cannot fully focus on the demons themselves all the time, as they need a lot of focus towards themselves too; so the lesser demons actually makes sense here, unlike in ULTRAKILL. That's super cool!
My only problem with the demon variety are the bosses, because they're really repetitive. Throughout the first 7 levels, it's the same exact boss used at the ending of them all. I just cannot defend that. And it's even worse when in 'Nihil' they decide to just throw two of those bosses in at the end at the same time... why? It's such a huge pace-breaker, due to how the difficulty suddenly rises by double. I shouted, and screamed in pure unfiltered anger so many times because of them. And it's even worse that when you fully die, you cannot just return to the boss itself... you need to replay the whole-ass level. BUT WHY?!?! I'm getting actual Dark Souls flashbacks here.
And it's EVEN worse when you finally beat them, the game never reaches that same difficulty level again. Not even with the final boss. That's SHOCKING. And I must say, that the final boss is really cool, and I think it may just be my favourite boss-fight in any FPS game to date. It was just so cool!

I really enjoyed this game, mostly. It has a lot of truly wonderful moments, and a plethora of fun hours at hand.
The campaign was quite fun, and really sweet. It uses some smart & unique map-designs which works surprisingly well, and something I haven't seem much of anywhere else. There's this section in the last mission, which really reminded me of the Resident Evil 4 staircase elevator section; and that was just amazing.
The main-campaign also creates a ton of cool set-pieces & twists; both visually & through game-play. I adored how the level 'Acheron' looks, it just might be my favourite. It has a hefty DOOM Eternal vibe.

I must admit that I got beat around a lot in this game, because my rhythm. However after a few levels I felt like I finally got the hang of it, like I finally got the rhythm of it all. And it begun to notice how each level has an entirely unique beat compared to the previous, which I felt was a smart move to change up the game-play as to prevent it being repetitive or stale; I can very much appreciate that.
But... there is one levels specifically with beats that just f#ck me up always, where its rhythm are totally in such a way where they for some reason do not compute in my brain. That one being 'Nihil'; which is a real bummer. I'm not sure if it's the music itself which has an unclear beat, of it's just the timing itself. But I could never really conjure that specific rhythm, and that honestly tilted me a lot, especially in its respective boss & Torment levels.

Most levels have 3 respective Torment levels, which are singular arenas with unique game-play twists. And honestly I enjoyed most of them, I really loved the 'Weapon Trickery' one specifically. That's a very smart game-play twist, as it caused moments otherwise unobtainable within the main-campaign itself, through its more limited focus to force you into learning each weapon through forcing you to use them. That's really cool, I hope more games do that. Yet the 'Slaughter Mastery' & 'Ultimate Mastery' piss me off.... a lot! Because in each Torment there's a time-limit, and you can gain more time by kills. Cool, neat. But when each wave of demons only spawn in by killing most/all other demons in the arena, it more often than not will cause you having to traverse to the opposite of the map just to get 1 specific kill, which can/will make you lose a ton of time or downright kill you. The amount of times my hand almost went through my monitor due to that is crazy. I really HATED those parts of Torments. Make waves of demons continuous, and instead of punishing players who cannot keep up by making them run out of time, kill them by flooding the room with demons.



[h1] Beatings & Beats [/h1]

The soundtrack of Metal: Hellsinger is really cool.
I've spent a lot of time listening to the soundtrack, both in-game & on YouTube (I beg you to add it on Spotify, dev)
And while there definitely are large curves in quality between them. The fan favourite no doubt being 'Stygia', 'Blood and Law', and 'No Tomorrow'; that's obvious. They're the best of the soundtrack, which is neat... But my problem is that they're the best because the rest are just 'cool' or 'good'. They're quite straightforward & typical. I wish the soundtrack was a lot more experimental, with more songs like 'Stygia' with a lot of clear vocals; much akin to musicians like Alcest's works. I also would've adored more experimental & boppy sounds like Turmion Kätilöt's line-up. Because the game is called "Metal: Hellsinger", not "Black Metal: Hellsinger"
Some smaller bands like Biomechanical would be very welcome.
And for a female protagonist, and for her to canonly be the vocals, as I understand it as... I'm quite shocked by how few of the vocals are actually sung by female leads. The male presence is of course fully welcome, yet females should've really been prioritized a lot more, in my humble opinion.
Still, even for all my hefty gripes, I still love most of it. I'm only being very critical & harsh because I love it & want it to be even better.

I also adore how each level is represented by art of which is supposed to look like vinyl covers full of marks & scratches. That blew my mind when I first noticed that, that was a really neat nod to the music itself, especially as each song is named after their respective level.



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

Metal: Hellsinger is a game I really enjoyed for the most part, and while there no doubt are moments I disliked a lot. The best parts not only overwhelm the negative ones, but leave a lengthier lasting impression as well. This game no doubt will land on my top 10 games of 2022! And I can't wait to replay it whenever I find the will to play it once more!

Rhythm game was never my type, but if you integrate it with shooting, that is a different story. The first game of this sub-genre I tried was BPM. It`s a fun game, yet something about it just didn`t click with me. So I try the subject of the review - Metal: Hellsinger, and I can confidently say that this game single-handedly ignite the spark of interest for the sub-genre for me. The rhythmic gameplay, the theme, and bonus challenges are really well-done. I highly recommend this game for those also looking to jump into the rhythmic shooters sub-genre.

[h1]Thing I Like About Metal: Hellsinger:[/h1]

[b]Combat, Arsenal, Music, EVERYTHING[/b]
Everything about this game is amazing.
→[b]Combat[/b]: I cannot stress enough how great it feels to shoot a gun in sync with rhythm of background music. This feature alone instills a certain flow of gameplay which is hard to recreate in other boomer shooters. Everything must be on beat. Bullets deal much more damage on beat. Shooting on beat grants more points. And music hypes up progressively as you do things on beat. All of this good traits form together a strong core gameplay loop that can easily pulls you in for hours.
→[b]Arsenal[/b]: Besides actions, Metal: Hellsinger also introduces 7 hellish armaments that each has its own unique flow of rhythm. Since all the weapons performs equally strong on beat, players can just choose whichever suits their playstyle. My favorite weapons of mass destruction are The Hounds and Hellcorw. Dual-wielding revolvers is something I can never pass up. Shooting these two bad boys on beat never gets old, and the dopamine never stops coming. Hellcrow, on the other hand, bounces off me at first. It`s weird beat and boomerang style really are my thing, until I dive in, giving it a shot. This weapon is actually a great multi-kill and crowd-control tools.
→[b]Music[/b]: Metal, as the music genre, is inherently compatible with extreme violence. Like Doom, Metal: Hellsinger has several blood-pumping soundtracks that merge wonderfully with on beat gameplay and demon-killing. One feature I have mentioned above is that as you build up the Fury meter, music gets progressively more hype-up. At maximum 16x, vocals start kicking in, and THAT is when the gameplay tension and immersion elevate to the utmost hype.

Metal: Hellsinger is what you get if you made an entire game revolve around the gore nest mechanic from DOOM 2016, and put some beat matching behind it. 

In short: it's fine. It's playable, it's good fun at times, and most of the songs go hard enough that, besides the obvious drive to try and keep the max combo multiplier going, you're also driven to keep it high enough that you can hear the backing track in its glorious entirety. The problem is that Metal: Hellsinger clearly designed itself around the new DOOM games and, consequently, suffers from constant nagging comparisons to that franchise - whereas DOOM's soundtrack ducks and swells with the chaotic action and extremely brief moments of peace around you, M:H's backing track stays (mostly) the same throughout the level, and indeed the whole game; whereas the glory kills in DOOM instill a sense of liberating violence, the 'slaughters' in M:H feel somewhat lifeless and weak; whereas the legions of hell in DOOM come in many shapes and sizes with all kinds of interesting mechanics and weak points, the enemies of M:H start off as somewhat uninspiring and only grow more tedious with exposure (I was particularly unimpressed with [spoiler]the final boss of each level being the same enemy with a slightly different gimmick each time[/spoiler]); whereas there is a constant back-and-forth in DOOM as you juggle your health and ammunition against those legions, you have infinite ammunition in M:H, health tends not to be much of a problem, and when it does become a problem there's a lot of conveniently placed wall crystals to heal from, which kinda defeats the point of having the slaughters/glory kills rewarding you with health in the first place.

Indeed, perhaps the biggest comparison-problem with M:H is that that back-and-forth in DOOM has an internal rhythm of itself - jump, dash, shoot, switch weapon, glory kill, jump, dash, grenade, rip, tear, etc etc; it's a masterpiece of game design that this internal rhythm is both set and felt by the player simultaneously, affording an experience that is completely unmatched in singleplayer FPS. In an act bordering on sacrilege, Metal: Hellsinger takes that experience, cuts out the most universally loved aspect of it, and instead forces the player to follow an external rhythm of their own design.

I really don't want to make it sound like i'm railing on this game for no reason, or that I didn't enjoy it - I did, I think it's worth your time, and while I think it has flaws it's still a solid game with a great soundtrack. It's just very difficult not to compare it to what it was clearly inspired by, especially where the design philosophy falls well short of its inspirations.

Metal Hellsinger is a first person shooter where the player is a demon trying to escape from hell. The unique gameplay twist is that you have to fire your guns in time to the beat of heavy metal music to build up your damage multiplier, allowing you to kill enemies quickly.

[h1]The Good[/h1]

•	Feels like an old school shooter where the movement is fast, there are lots of enemies in each encounter, and you have to always be moving to avoid taking damage.

•	The beat matching gameplay mechanic is fun. I found that I didn’t really have to look at the on screen timing indicator, I was able to use my ears to track the beat, so my eyes could focus on aiming at the demons.

•	There are four main weapons including dual pistols, shotgun, explosive crossbow and dual throwing axes. I mostly used the shotgun because its click click boom click click boom firing speed is a close match to the music beat, while the pistols’ longer effective range makes them more useful against bosses.

•	A couple of other mechanics add a tactical element to the combat. Successful attacks build up your weapon’s ultimate meter, allowing you to use a special attack powerful enough to one hit kill most enemies, which I would save for the more dangerous demons. And when an enemy is near death, you can press a button to quickly fly over and execute them, causing them to drop shards which restore your health (similar to the modern Doom games).

•	I played on the medium (“goat”) difficulty because I wasn’t sure how tricky the beat matching mechanic would be. Regular encounters can get intense on the later levels, while the bosses are quite challenging because of their bullet hell style attacks.

•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes or framerate. Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

[h1]The Bad[/h1]

•	The game is incredibly short, as I completed it in just 3.4 hours. It seems like the developers intend the player to replay the same levels over and over again chasing high scores for the leaderboards, which isn’t really what I’m looking for in a single player FPS, although I suppose I’ll have to do it to salvage some value for money.

[h1]The Recommendation[/h1]

If you like your shooters fast and your music loud, Metal Hellsinger is definitely the game for you. Its just a massive shame that the game is so short, and because of this I can only recommend it on a deep sale.

I’d love to have an optional third-person mode. The protagonist looks great, but during actual gameplay we barely get to see her. It also feels like a missed opportunity for the skins — what’s the point of choosing a cool look if you can’t really see it in action? Being able to switch between first- and third-person views would make both the character design and cosmetics much more enjoyable.

Hellsinger is a short game clocking in about 4 hours to beat, but the game is rich in atmosphere.
The primary drive of the game is, of course, its soundtrack which features the likes of Serj Tankian from System of a Down and Randy Blythe from Lamb of God among a dozen others in the metal music industry. Those into the music of games like Doom and Devil May Cry will find a home here for that reason alone.
Its gameplay is rather interesting being an FPS, Rhythm title that my best way to describe is 'Dancing in Doom' which itself is a novelty as hit combos and different move unlocks to add to its variety. The short length means it never gets the chance to get stale which is both a blessing and curse but the combat being tuned to the music beat is fun and adds in a grain of challenge that keeps the player's agency to their movements and attacks that keeps things fun.
There are side activities with torments and the game is open to modding with a means to import .wav sound files into the game (any music file works, not just metal music) and incorporates the BPM that the gameplay is tuned into which can add hours, though mileage will vary of course for such a short game.

If you like metal music and/or demon slaying it's worth giving it a look. Just keep in mind you are getting a short game with mod support, unique gameplay, and a headbanger of a soundtrack. If that sounds alright with you, check it out.

[h2] \m/ [/h2]

The concept is simple and rarely seen at this production level. The game's premise is simple, you are in Hell and must fight a horde of demons to find your voice again stolen by the Underlord himself. While the story starts as an exciting concept, it sadly is a complete afterthought. Unmemorable at best, there is little to do throughout the game about character development despite all the interesting elements you encounter throughout your playthrough.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2959616033

You are not grabbing Metal: Hellsinger for its story; you are here because it's a Rhythm game, and it's achieving that exceptionally well. You need to follow the tempo set by both visual and sound cues. On top of that, to attain peak headbanging status, you will have to ensure that you don't lose the combos you are building. Each level has its particular soundtrack that keeps building up the more you kill, dodge, reload, and jump on the beat to let the vocals be heard finally. I don't think there's anything more satisfying than the drums connecting with a properly timed reload+headshot

You will also get to use finishers ala Doom to regain lost health, and ammunitions are infinite so that you can focus on the action. The controls are very intuitive and easy to take on, and we must applaud the developers for the accessibility features included in the game that are going to make sure that everyone gets to enjoy the game.

It would be impossible to review this game without talking about the soundtrack. It is one of the best I've heard in a video game. Two Feathers, a studio focused on video game music, delivered a phenomenal product with the help of famous Metal singers ranging from Arch Enemy, Dark Tranquility to Trivium, Lamb of God etc. The singers also did an outstanding job on each track, and the music is seamlessly integrated into the gameplay; the result is an incredibly immersive experience.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2959616083

Graphically speaking, the themes are exactly what you would expect from hell, dark, gothic, and satanic, with each demon being different and identifiable. 

Sadly, the game is short, and the level design is all the same level after level. The boss fights especially, it’s all the same enemy with little variations, and even though there are some challenges to extend the game's length, it’s not quite that. Though, it must be said that the game is infinitely replayable if you want to compete for leaderboards. Indeed you can compare your score with other players, improve on it and keep headbanging.

Finally, Metal: Hellsingers is a fun and unique game that will appeal to both metal fans and rhythm gamers, and while it is short, the spectacular soundtrack and gameplay make up for it.

[h1]Overview:[/h1]
This game is fun for the first two hours, then the novelty immediately wears off.
[h2]Modes:[/h2]
[h3]Main Story[/h3]
The campaign is repetitive - go to this location, kill enemies here, rinse and repeat with barely any changes to gameplay flow or enemy roster. They introduce a couple new weapons in the first levels but other than that it's the same thing. Literally - they recycle the same stage boss 5 or 6 times at [b]LEAST[/b] ([i]Did the developers take inspiration from Halo 5 Guardian?[/i]).
Overall, the campaign is rather short, so it ends just as things start to get really annoyingly repetitive.
As for the story itself - well, it's an interesting jab at the classical religious portrayal of Heaven and Hell, it's more or less a diet coke version of DOOM Eternal's implementation.
You play as a female demon who lost her voice and is in a relentless uphill battle against overwhelming odds to reclaim it. Along the way, you meet Paz, your sidekick and the narrative voice of reason throughout your quest who has a southern cowboy accent. 
The judge is the keeper of Hell(s) and upon killing her you break through the barrier between Hell, Reality (Earth) and Heaven.

[h3]Leviathan:[/h3]
Ugh, where do I even begin with this mess of a mode? Remember when I said the main story got repetitive and that was it's biggest flaw? Well, if you touch this mode you'll think the story is x10 times more fun. 
Why, you may ask? Simple.
You are stripped of ALL your abilities. Let me rephrase - [b]ALL[/b].
That means no primary or secondary weapons - you only have your starter weapons: the borderline useless skull and your blade ([i]which here, most enemies will be ranged ones and most encounters will drain you of your health and considering how scarce health is, that is NOT a viable option to get into the later stages[/i]).
You have no DASH and your movement speed is severely impacted to make traversing the tiny-ass maps slower in order to not make you immediately notice how minuscule these set-pieces are. 
And to add insult to injury, you cannot perform glory kills to gain health back, you're essentially reliant on the crystal health drops but once those are gone, you're boned. 
The only things to help you long term are upgrading your health upgrades. (One increases Max HP, others increase crystal spawns which doesn't honestly help all that much and there is one perk that allows you to regen health when standing still, however it is painfully slow and borderline useless since you cannot regen between rounds either.
With this in mind, enemies that you would mop the floor with such as the acid flies now are complete game-enders 'cause if you get caught in the acid you're slowed down even more ([i]if you don't pick the upgrade at the Altar which I'll get into in a second[/i]).
The Altar: Okay so this is your typical horde/survival mode vendor/shop in between waves. You charge up the altar by killing enemies and once the meter is full it sends out a wave that kills any remaining enemies.
The Altar will randomly give you a selection of 3 perks (4 if you have the upgrade).
 ([i]These can be an increase to your damage, damage absorption, another weapon, or misc perks that make enemies bleed or explode[/i])
You can only pick one perk per round.
So yeah, Leviathan is an unfair pile of garbage EVEN with a all of the upgrades.

[h3]Speaking of upgrades:...[/h3]
You can collect Void Coins in order to upgrade your abilities to make Leviathan mode even barely remotely fair.
You have questionably complex skill trees for a game like this and you can upgrade either your health, weapons, abilities, etc.
Considering you're spending loads of points on for example upgrading your revolvers, you'd expect the game to allow you to keep them permanently after maxing them out, but no, you're given one more wave to keep them before they expire ([i]alongside damage and fury bonuses[/i]).
There are only a handful of actually useful upgrades such as increasing your max health, adding back dash from the start (it should have been there to begin with, but I digress), enabling your ultimate or even increasing the amount of perks you can choose from from 3 to 4.
Most upgrades are very pricey considering that you have to painful sit through and grind through with barely anything at the beginning. (for instance most upgrades are at min 20 points, max 150 pts and around 30-50 per average, finishing about 8 waves will get you 20 void coins to upgrade so it will take a VERY long time).
To make matters more interesting you are capped at a max of 3000 points allocated total - this means you CANNOT exceed this range with your upgrades, so if you somehow manage to get a lot of points and are thinking of unlocking all the upgrades, no dice - you have to create a build and go with it.
I respect the dedication to make such an intricate system, however if it is rigged against the player to this degree with such an abrupt curve in progression then there is absolutely no incentive to play the game to progress. At the end of the day, this is just a rhythm-based first person shooter.

[h3]Loadout[/h3]
The game allows you to set up your loadout, which is only really useful in Story Mode since in Leviathan you're starting more or less bare-handed.
You can change your outfit or weapons (The game has about 8 weapons)
[list]
[*]Useless-ass Skull (it shoots fireballs)
[*]Blade
[*]Shotgun (slow, but pretty meaty)
[*]Dual Revolvers (really fun)
[*]Crossbow (that has AOE, probably one of the best weapons in the game)
[*]Throwable Dual Blade Staffs (pretty slow and eh)
[*]Gatling Gun (its alright, but literally using the revolvers/crossbow is the meta)
[*]DLC Bow
[/list]

[h3]Conclusions:[/h3]
I got this game while it was on sale, however after an unsatisfying short and repetitive campaign and a horrible horde mode, I still feel robbed of $10. 
The concept of the game is solid, the gameplay is there, it just needs way more thought put behind it and a lot more refining. The developers have the soul for their game but somehow dropped the ball and implemented so many questionable design decisions that stained that great first impression I have and left me with a bitter taste.
The only pros I can think of is that the DLC contains songs from Disturbed, Gorillaz (Don't ask me how or why) and Muse.
Purchase when on sale, otherwise don't bother, it is not worth your time unless it is patched sometime in the future.

I'm not sure why they went with a two (additional) weapon limit given the old school arena design, but I found the dual pistol + shotgun loadout to be more than enough for every level. Levels are completely linear. There's no exploration, no puzzles, no secrets (that I could find), and little to no challenging platforming sections. There's barely any level hazards besides some extremely weak lava. It doesn't need these things, but it could've helped make the very short levels a little longer. Each level can be finished in like 10-20 minutes and there's only 8 levels (Hells) with 3 optional challenges (Torments) per level. Even on the highest difficulty, this game is a breeze. It ramps up near the end, but unless you're inert or rhythmically challenged, you should have ZERO issue blasting through this game. Health is PLENTIFUL considering there are health pickups around the arena and all enemies can be executed for health. It needs another difficulty option. Maybe two more. For the positives, the game looks beautiful and runs smooth, as it should given it's rhythm based design. Once I got the audio latency right with my shitty speakers, I had no issue staying on beat. The soundtrack is the highlight here. It's heavy and you WILL headbang on every level. All the weapons look and feel distinct with powerful special abilities for all of them. There's good enemy variety, but their designs are boring. Just looks like Doom leftovers. While the levels look cool, they're forgettable visually. Again, just looks like Doom leftovers. I think this is more of an issue with the industry as a whole designing Hell to be the same old horned-demon, lava spewing, fire breathing, red, red, very RED look over and over again. You can only do so much with that art style. I enjoy the game, but it's unexceptional IN MY OPINION. If you want an arbitrary score, I'll give it a 6/10.

just go play Bullets Per Minute instead. It does the rhythm shooter angle so much better than this. It does it so much better I even have a list.

1. You cannot fire on half-beats. This is by far the biggest mistake this game makes. By counting half-beats, BPM feels like it has a faster pace and makes it more forgiving as you can just hop right back into the beat instead of having to wait and ultimately missing it. BPM even counts quarter beats at some points depending on your equipment.
2. Reloading feels much slower than BPM because you only need to hit the reload button once. In BPM, you MUST hit the reload button multiple times (more or less depending on the gun) in order to complete the reload. In this you just hit it once on the beat and you can't fire for a couple beats until your character is done. It does allow you to hit it a second time to make it go by faster, but that doesn't excuse it.
3. You can still shoot off-beat, albeit with little to no damage. It's good that it does almost no damage, but simply being able to fire off-beat at all will cause the player to make more mistakes, as instead of frantically trying to get back on-beat you just wait until your slight difference in beat catches up.
4. The music is MUCH worse from a rhythm standpoint. I did not say it's bad, it's pretty good all things considered, but it did not have as strong a base as BPM's. In BPM, I could count every beat by the song alone no matter the situation. In this, I often lose track of the beat because the game is too busy screaming into my ears and playing guitar riffs (not like I'd find the beat anyway when the drums are going so fast). I'll also add that the enemies not attacking on-beat makes this even worse because I can't follow their actions to get on-beat either.
5. The beat tracker is sometimes hard to read. This may just be me being stupid, but I find the beat tracker to be way too busy. It shows the shadow of my shots so I know how far off I was, but it just ends up confusing me due to their size and length. BPM did it right by making it so that the beat tracker just turns red and continues if I make a mistake. It's so much simpler and easy to read.
6. The narrator can be annoying sometimes. This isn't related to gameplay, but I find narrators interrupting the game to tell me exactly what the character is thinking instead of what I think she's thinking is just a dumb decision. There's a moment in the second level when a mysterious monster flees behind a corner. I thought to myself "I wonder what that was, guess I'll follow it to find out", and then the narrator chimed in to tell me the exact thing I was thinking. Just let me think for the character please.
7. BPM has much more varied gameplay. It has many different characters and difficulties to pick from, and adds their own challenges that change how you have to play. Hellsinger does nothing of the sort, but I guess that might just be because BPM is a roguelike. At least you can start with different loadouts.
8. I could tell that from a pure enemy and level design standpoint that this game is easier than BPM. This game has a long tutorial that explains super simple mechanics (for a person that's played rhythm games and shooter games before), and BPM has no tutorial at all outside a practice mode. Most of the difficulty comes from how frustrating the controls are compared to BPM for all the reasons listed above. I died within 5 minutes in BPM, and soon got good enough to beat the next couple of bosses within 15-ish minutes. I got through two stages without dying in Hellsinger, and I didn't improve by playing these stages.

This does not mean the game is without its perks though. Here's a couple I could think of in the small span I'm writing this.
1. The inclusion of melee weapons is such a no-brainer I'm surprised BPM didn't include it at all. I'd prefer if it was bound to a single key like borderlands, but this works perfectly fine.
2. The weapons are pretty nice. I always like dual-wielded revolvers and was pleasantly surprised to see them in the trailer and game. I'm sure there's many more interesting weapons later in the game that I didn't get to see.
3. It's nice that it has an actual story. BPM never even attempted at a plotline. You just go through a dungeon and kill a dragon. I especially like the narrator's voice, even though he often rudely interrupts the gameplay so I can hear what the character's thinking. If the voice was confined to just cutscenes it would make it much more tolerable.
4. The graphics are much more refined than BPM's. Obviously this is due to the game's budget and the it looks much better, but I don't think it feels as inspired as BPM's. BPM's graphics are very stylized with it's cell-shaded high-saturated look. Hellsinger's looks much better, but it mostly feels like a rehash of doom. This isn't helped by it being a journey through hell.
5. The player character is much cooler looking than most of the valkyries in BPM. I'm a bit of a sucker for demonic character design and this character really hits that for me. Still not as good as Gery though, nothing is.

I will say that this is not a bad game. As much as I rag on it, I think it's a worthwhile game for many to play seeing it's a much more mainstream approach to a rhythm shooter. I mostly criticize all this because I think BPM is more worth your time than this because of it's much more fun gameplay and better-integrated rhythm mechanics. In some ways this feels like the comparison between Doom Eternal and Ultrakill. Ultrakill is a much more fast-paced and skill oriented shooter than Doom, and BPM is a much more fast-paced and skill oriented rhythm shooter than Hellsinger. Hellsinger even has glory kill animations
